newsitem.title: GERMANY: German film feted as opening act of Berlin fest.
newsitem.headline: German film feted as opening act of Berlin fest.

text.p: A big budget German film, the thriller "Smilla's Sense of Snow", was given the rare honour on Thursday of opening the 47th annual Berlin Film Festival.

Paying tribute to Germany's revived domestic film industry, the 12-day festival that in past years often ignored German films raised the curtains with the German-Danish co-production from Munich's Bernd Eichinger.
The $35 million English-language detective story set in Denmark stars Julie Ormond, Richard Harris and Vanessa Redgrave. It was the first German-made film to open the festival in 10 years.

More than 3,000 journalists and 8,000 directors, producers, actors and film buyers from around the world are attending the Berlinale, considered the industry's second most important gathering after the Cannes festival in May.
"I feel very honoured that this film was selected to open the festival," said Eichinger, the head of Constantin Film whose earlier worldwide hits include "The House of Spirits".
"Smilla's Sense of Snow" was directed by Denmark's Bille August and also features many leading German actors such as Mario Adorf and Juergen Vogel.
"This is an international film, but it is also a German film and not just because of the financing but because we developed the creative elements," said Eichinger.

The film. based on a best-selling Danish novel, is the story of a scientist played by Ormond who suspects foul play in the death of a six-year-old boy. Against improbable odds, she tracks down the killers in Greenland.

Aside from 25 films competing for the "Golden Bear" awards to be presented at the end of the festival on February 24, 300 films from 60 countries not in competition are being screened in theatres across Berlin.
Another 400 films are being viewed by film buyers working for international distributors and television networks at the European Film Market running alongside the Berlinale.

Heading the films making their international debuts is "The English Patient", which received 12 Academy Award nominations including Best Picture in Los Angeles on Tuesday. It was the early favourite for the Golden Bear.

Other films in the running for Oscar awards being screened for the first time outside the United States are "The Crucible" and "The People vs Larry Flynt", both of which received two Acadmemy Award nominations.

The opening-act tribute to "Smilla's Sense of Snow" represented a further boost to the red-hot German market. After decades of decline, the rejuvenated local film industry has become one of the world's fastest-growing.

It is still far away from recapturing the cinematic glory of the fabled Babelsberg studios era in the 1920s and 30s, when German-made films such as Fritz Lang's "Metropolis" and "The Blue Angel" starring Marlene Dietrich were shown around the world.

But it is the world's second largest behind only the United States with 1.3 billion marks in ticket sales. A string of German-language box office hits has set international standards in beating back Hollywood's once-insurmountable domination.

"A lot of things are happening in Germany," said Eichinger. "The public's faith in German filmmakers is returning and the filmmakers are regaining the confidence that they can make films the public wants to see. The public (for German films) was always there. We just didn't deliver the product."

Eichinger's latest German-language hit, a satire about Munich's film scene called "Rossini", took $8.4 million at the box office in its first two weeks and jumped to the top of the German charts ahead of seven Hollywood films.
